utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped yesterday talking about those buildings that were detonated and the events that happened earlier. All this combined caused great anxiety among the Serbian population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, from what I see from your statement, the issue of how to obtain weapons became very topical. You explain that on the 13th of May, 1991 you took over a certain amount of weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, "The blue Zastava vehicle appeared, reduced speed, somebody dumped ammunition, and the vehicle drove on"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know these people who brought this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this given to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just dumped outside from a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was around when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you took the weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I see here that you were arrested because of this. How did it come about, your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took the weapons, I was arrested on my way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you spent time in a prison in Osijek; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a regular prison, an investigations prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigations prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you tried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was released in the course of an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were exchanged on that occasion? How many of you were in that prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many we were, but there was a busload of people who were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You personally have knowledge only about the group with whom you were exchanged; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Since this was a regular investigations prison in Osijek, how were you treated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody mistreated you, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no rough treatment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see -- you say on page 3 of your statement, at the very beginning of the first paragraph: "In the Osijek prison, I was very roughly treated. During interrogation, I was beaten up very badly on several occasions. The same happened to a number of other Serb prisoners that were there with me."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I added that to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you amended your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it wasn't recorded correctly the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this another thing that hadn't been properly -- properly recorded, what it says in the next paragraph: "For a number of days after I came back home, I was unable to go out for several days because I was in such a bad shape." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it really so or is this an error?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mentally in such a bad shape. Physically, I was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you tried to find your family, who lived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You had heard that the JNA had evacuated them from Vukovar and you found them in the second half of the month of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say -- I don't know about this term, because I see it in your statement for the first time, "The so-called space police arrested all the non-Serb residents." What kind of police is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sort of self-styled police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean a para-police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it consisted of who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three or four men at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were arresting non-Serb residents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they people from Dalj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your own local people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from what I understand, they were neither members of the JNA nor members of any other formation. You could call them some sort of self-appointed, self-styled police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, self-appointed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a certain person by the name of Stricevic, who was the chief of police in Dalj; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of this space police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was the chief of this illegal police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, because you seem to have spent only a month with the Territorial Defence, what was the reason why you left the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to go back to my job and my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 3, in this large, long paragraph: "I needed fuel for my car, but I couldn't buy it without a voucher issued by the TO commander. I asked Pavle Milovanovic, also known as Pajo, to issue me with this voucher, but he refused. This upset me, so I decided to leave the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you left the TO because this so-called Pajo, the commander, refused to issue you with a voucher for fuel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me a little more, in greater detail about this person from Vukovar who was brought to the police station in Dalj and who, according to your statement, used the building of the old farm cooperative. It must be some sort of farm, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your statement correctly - and I'll read out from page 4 - "I heard that one group of people had also been brought to the Dalj police station, which at that time was using the building of the old cooperative centre as their station. But I personally did not see these people." You didn't see this personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard from someone else that these people had been brought to the building of the agricultural cooperative?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say - and I have the impression that these are two separate things - you say that you were trying to help some people, to get them out of prison, some among the people who were detained there. Are we talking about a different place, a different prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A different place and a different prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the prison located in the very local commune, in the TO headquarters, and there was another prison located at the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went there and you managed to free a couple of people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said a moment ago that it was a TO prison organised or set up by local residents. We established that much at the beginning of your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA had nothing to do with it; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you continued to speak about the first killing in Dalj, when one of the prisoners who had been detained and interrogated there jumped out of the window, as you say, and was then killed by a TO guard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was that guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an older man, known under the nickname Babura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know this man. He is a local resident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now something about this group of people who were killed. You mentioned that they had been on a slope somewhere between Dalj and Lovas; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the Lovas farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So at the Lovas farm. Do you know anything about the circumstances under which they were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I heard when I came there was that they had been brought by bus and that this was done by people from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you would be kind enough to explain this in greater detail a little more clearly, because I see on page 6 of your statement that this commander, the man who was there with you, told you that they had been killed by Savuljasi men. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the name of a street near Borovo Selo. It belongs to the territory of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a group of men named after a street in Borovo Selo, and he explained to you that they -- this group of people had been killed by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he also explain that they had been brought there and executed by firing squad, or did he say anything more precisely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they had been brought by some bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no doubt that all of them were killed there on the spot and they had not been brought from anywhere.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the bodies, I believe they were killed on that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, regarding these people brought from Vukovar, what actually happened to them? Because in the course of the examination-in-chief, I heard you describing how a large number of residents of Vukovar was brought there. What do you mean by "large number"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, about three truckloads, which means 60 to 70 people, were brought to the building of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to say that the women were taken to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They just took their names down, listed them, and transported them to Serbia after they had spent only one night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who transported them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken there by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand the vehicle used was a bus, but I mean who did this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the TO transported them to Serbia after they were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many men were they -- were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Red Cross building, there were only women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were only transported and released on the other side. How about the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men were at the TO, in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the place where you went to intervene for a couple of them to be released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same number; 50 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those men who were at the local commune, that is, the TO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also transferred to the cinema hall in Dalj, and from then on they were also transported by buses to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say they too were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any of them mistreated or killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was mistreatment, but I don't know that anybody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you managed to release only a few, and the rest were released. But how much later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more or less two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone interrogate them in the meantime and then release them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, since in the examination-in-chief you were asked in connection with cooperation between the TO or, rather, the locals who were in Dalj with the JNA. And I gathered from your explanations that the JNA had a unit in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A JNA headquarters in Ilok was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a headquarters in the PP Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they asked you whether the TO cooperated with the JNA, and you said that you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many JNA members were there in this PP Dalj? What is that PP Dalj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An agricultural enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was it a platoon, a company, a unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were within the PP Dalj compound. That is where their vehicles were stationed. There were guards in front of the gate so that people couldn't enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But there were no prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly there was a group of civilians from Vukovar up there in a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly they, too, were taken to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether any of them were mistreated by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1175. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, during this cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic asked you about the arming of the Croats. And in your statement that forms part of your testimony, you said that you heard stories that the Croats were arming themselves, that you did not see that but that you saw a truck and concluded that the stories were true. And my question to you is: Who actually told such stories about the arming of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were telling those stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also get stories of that kind from the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, during his cross-examination, also asked you about events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991. Were you in Borovo Selo at that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you personally make any observation related to the events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. Only the people from Dalj headed towards Borovo Selo to see what was going on, so that we heard everything from them. Some of them even went into Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those who informed you about the events, were they all Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you get also information about the events in -- in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian television carried reports, as did the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatian television report also the killing of 12 policemen, Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have any means to check whether the reports that you heard from people or from the media were correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic also put to you other events related to Borovo Selo in April and May 1991. Did you observe any of these events yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the source of your information to these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every event that happened, shall we say in Borovo Selo, the people in the village heard about it straight away, so that I obtained all the information from the locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic also asked you about what happened to certain groups of people that were brought from Vukovar, and my question to you is: What happened to those that you saw being detained in that prison behind the TO headquarters? Do you know what became of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what became of them or where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long were they kept there? Also only for a few days, or longer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they beat them and mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This svemirska police, or cosmic police, and this group that came from Prigrevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also -- and you also mentioned the people that were detained or you heard about in the Dalj police building. What became of them? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1175 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that there was a story one day that some of them were killed at Jama, down the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the questions that the Prosecution has. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1175, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. If you'd just wait for the blinds to be lowered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness leaves, I would like to announce a -- a change in the witness list, or, rather, a drop in the witness list, just so that the parties do not prepare. The witness Josipovic will not be called this week, and we will re-evaluate whether we will have to call him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The next witness is which, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness will be Witness C-1071.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told there's one witness who may have difficulty in reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right? Is this the witness, do we know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe it is the following witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps while we're waiting, if I could ask the registrar to place this sheet on the table where the witness will sit, containing her true name. Thank you very much. While we're waiting, Your Honours, Witness C-1071 will discuss events that relate to page 23 of the Croatia atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. There's a matter I need to consult on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to go into private session to deal with the voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry to put you through that, but could you take the declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, good morning. There is a piece of paper in front of you. And without reading the name that is on that piece of paper, could you simply please verify that that is your true name written on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During this proceeding this morning, I will refer to you by the pseudonym C-1071.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness C-1071, did you provide a statement to a member of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in May of 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the past few days, have you had the opportunity to review the statement that you gave in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And two days ago, did you confirm to an officer of the Registry of this Tribunal that your statement is true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would offer the statement of this witness into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. We have provided a redacted version for the public and an unredacted version to be filed under seal. There is a passport photo that is attached to this statement, and that should be filed under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get the next exhibit number for the package.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the end of the battle for Vukovar on 19 November 1991, JNA soldiers escorted Witness C-1071, her husband, who was a Croat, and their two children from the basement of their apartment building to the village of Luzac. In Luzac, Serb forces separated men from women and children and the men were taken to the local community building in Luzac. Witness C-1071 last saw her husband when she handed him some cigarettes by this building. Shortly thereafter, the JNA transported Witness C-1071 and her children to the village of Brsadin and from there civilian buses carried them to Bac in Vojvodina in the Republic of Serbia. Witness C-1071 subsequently heard that many people from Vukovar were taken to the village of Dalj, and she made several trips to Dalj to search for her husband. She spoke to people at the JNA headquarters in Dalj, the Territorial Defence headquarters in Dalj, the Dalj police, and the local Red Cross. No one gave her any information about the fate or whereabouts of her husband. However, one man who resided in Dalj told Witness C-1071 that he had seen her husband in front of the Red Cross building in Dalj and that her husband had been beaten. Another person told Witness C-1071 that she should stop looking for her husband because he had been killed. This person, however, did not give Witness C-1071 any more information. Seven to eight years after she last saw her husband, another person gave information to Witness C-1071. This person told Witness C-1071 that her husband was seen in front of the Dalj cinema. A man approached and said, "I need this one." A guard told the man that Witness 1071's husband had "passed the procedure." But the man insisted that he wanted Witness C-1071's husband and returned with a group of men. They captured Witness C-1071's husband inside the Dalj cinema and took him away. Later, gunshots were heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the examination, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, if you have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam 1071, you lived in Vukovar throughout, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that from the second half of August 1991 the situation in Vukovar became very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And actually, that you found yourself in the midst of a military operation, because there was fighting everywhere around you. Could you be kind enough to describe -- can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes. No, I can't hear again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to describe that situation. What was it that changed? How did this dangerous situation come about? You were in Vukovar throughout, even before that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: How can I describe it? Shooting started, barricades. Simply, it became dangerous for everyone. Around the 24th of August onwards, everything was blocked, so that we couldn't go anywhere from Vukovar, and our life was reduced to our own -- the confines of our own apartment. My family spent the whole time in the basement, that is, for 86 days I and the children were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when did the fighting in Vukovar start and this irregular state of affairs, the tensions and everything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Sometime in the spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: People were arming themselves. They were erecting barricades. Simply, it wasn't safe anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was arming themselves and who was putting up these barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I personally don't know. I heard that everyone was doing it. Now, who is everyone? Around Vukovar, in the villages, the villages were separating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were living in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But I was living in an apartment building, so that I didn't have information about it, only from the media, while we still had power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any idea as to what was happening in your town? Or you didn't leave the building at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I didn't leave the building, but I heard from people who did move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: That there were various acts of sabotage, shooting, arrests, blockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What shooting? What act of sabotage? What kind of incidents and events had you heard about? I assume you must remember something about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I heard about certain premises that were being blown up, that there was shooting at certain houses. I just heard about this; I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these premises that were blown up were owned by Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those business premises that were blown up in the period starting with March, when the conflict started, up until the time when they escalated in August, as you say, do you know anything at all about the crimes that were being committed against the Serbs in Vukovar throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I heard about them. There were stories. But as I say, I didn't leave my apartment after August, so I simply don't know. This is just unverified information. And I did hear that the most frequent victims were people in mixed marriages. I don't know how to put it. I can't claim that with certainty, because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that sometime in July, before those events escalated further, that the president of the municipality was replaced? He was a Serb. His name was Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the reasons for his replacement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Again, I don't know personally. I'm not a politician. People were saying that it was because he was a Serb, and that someone else was appointed in his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You listened to the radio, and do you remember that at the time the director of the radio was replaced too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: It was Radio Vukovar at the time. Later on it became Croatian Radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, it was Radio Vukovar at the time and then Croatian Radio.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the liquidations of Serbs in Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: As I said, I heard about that. We were a mixed population, and there were rumours going around to that effect. But I didn't see this or read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you neither saw it nor read about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the village of Brsadin, which was just mentioned, near Vukovar on the 1st of May, 1991, the first Serb victim fell?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness [sic] didn't catch the name of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A man called Djuro Gelincin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I don't know. I just heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the paramilitary units that were set up, that committed those murders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I don't know where they were set up, where they gathered or where they ambushed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the collection centres for Serbs in Vukovar? According to my information, you were a citizen of Vukovar, so you would certainly be aware of that. The collection centres in Borovo Komerc, Borovo Nova Obuca, the hangar at the airport, the unfinished school in Borovo, the kindergarten in the municipality, in the municipality basement, in the atomic shelter, in Drvo Promet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I heard about all that after the war, when we came back, when the fighting started. People were talking about this. But I wasn't there. I didn't see that. I did not see a single victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, you say, "When I came back." When did you come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: On the 27th or 28th of November, 1991, some ten days later, after the fighting had stopped. People talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the places where Serbs were killed after interrogation and arrest? For example, Trpinska Cesta, Borovska Cesta, Zracni Klub Borovo, the Borovo stadium, the Pcelica Creche, the bank of the Danube, and so on and so forth. I have quite a long list here, so I won't burden you with the whole list. Did you hear about these locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: All the locations are familiar to me. I heard about this, but I didn't see it because I had other things to do, and it was terrible even to hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Terrible even to hear about it. Did you hear about Marko Filkovic, known as Kinez, who was the commander of the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear a single name of the people killed under his command, the civilians, especially November 1991, early November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I heard some names later on, but -- well, maybe those people I knew, but the names meant nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an event when in the house of Milos Novakovic, in which whole families were hiding in the basement, the Pavlovic family, the Pavic family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Where is this street? Where is this house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, the house belongs to Milos Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes. But where is it? I don't know. I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were still in Vukovar in August 1991, do you remember in Olajnica, in the atomic shelter, some children were killed or, rather, slaughtered, 15-year-old boys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know about the atomic shelter in Olajnica but I wasn't there and I didn't hear about this event. I heard later on that some children were killed by a shell which landed in front of the shelter, and this was just before the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the blockade of the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: The barracks is quite far from the area where I live. People said it had been blocked, that water, power, and food had been cut off, and that attacks on Vukovar had started for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about shooting at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: It's too far from where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at least when the blockade started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know that from the 24th of August on I didn't leave my basement, because that's when the planes started flying over. And they said that a truck had been attacked on its way to Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it started before that date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the JNA tolerated all this until the 1st of October and took no action, expecting the barracks to be unblocked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to answer your questions, but I had two children to look after. And as I have already told you, I didn't leave the basement at all after the 24th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that two JNA soldiers arrived and told you you were to leave. Did they do this to protect you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they help you to take shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: They protected us while we crossed the street to come to a house where we would be safe. One went in front of us and one went behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say they took you to a soccer field where there were already a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see your husband there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: My husband came with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were all together then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they detain him there? From what you said in your statement, I understood that he was in a logistics group for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was working there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: All the men, both young and elderly men, were separated off on that soccer field. The women were left behind, and the men were taken to the school and the local commune for their documents to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what Mr. Saxon said, I understood that after this you never saw your husband again. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So everything you learnt, you learned while searching for him from your conversations with some people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to know more about the last part of Mr. Saxon's explanation. You said that from a certain person, whose name I will not mention so as not to identify you, that this person saw your husband in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that this person said that they were taken to Dalj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: We all passed through Dalj, but I passed through Dalj earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading what it says here: "The person was standing in front of the cinema in Dalj when my husband approached them."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is about your husband.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "They chatted for a while, when a rather short man approached my husband and told him he needed him."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say, "The men who were guarding the area told him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that my husband had gone through the procedure and he had been released."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1071, could you please explain: When you were separated off, you were protected by the JNA; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It follows from this that some sort of check was carried out and that your husband was released by the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, as far as Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The people you mention as trying to capture your husband again or do something to him had nothing to do with the JNA; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: That's what transpires from what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they local people from Dalj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that this man insisted, although he had been told that the man had been released, and then he brought another group of people, who captured him and took him away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the last you heard of your husband; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify this. Did you ever see members of the JNA behaving illegally or using violence against people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't keep you long. I know this is not easy for you. I want to clarify just a few more points. You spent some time in Serbia with relatives.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't mention the place, it doesn't matter. It was in Vojvodina, in the north part of Serbia. Did you try through the Red Cross in that municipality or the Red Cross of Serbia or the International Red Cross to obtain some information? Did you apply for help to any authorities in that municipality in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No. I went back to Dalj on my own, to search.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you crossed the Danube to search for your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes. The children remained in Serbia and I went back to search for my husband through the police, the territorials, the army. They said that they would check and that he would follow us after being checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's what was supposed to happen, because he was released after the check and then he was captured by some people. From these conversations, did you understand that he was captured by a group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: That's what I understood. In fact, I understood that he disappeared because he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what prison your husband was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: As far as I know, he never went further than Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dalj was held by the TO of Dalj, or the Dalj police; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you heard that in front of the Red Cross building your husband was beaten.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to find out who these men were who captured your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I didn't apply to the units there because it was hard for me to say that my husband was a Croat and because I was left on my own with my daughters. The man who told me that my husband had been killed in Dalj told me to calm down and to stop looking for the sake of my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before you met this acquaintance of yours who told you that he had gone through the procedure and been released --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- were you able to pinpoint the time referred to by the man who told you that your husband had been killed and the time when the person who talked to him in front of the cinema saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: This man, when I was searching through Dalj -- because I went to Dalj every day begging for information, trying to find out. And if my husband had been killed, trying to find his body to bury him. This was in 1991. As nobody wanted to talk about such things, a year had elapsed before that woman described the last moments of my husband's life. She was probably afraid for her own safety or maybe she was afraid she would have to testify, but nobody told me that they had seen my husband being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that before you met this acquaintance of yours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The last part of the question was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, this person died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you what the person's name was, even if we have to go into closed session, because this person would have to know more about this. He would have to know who did this and how and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt and deal with this. We didn't get the interpretation of the person to whom you were referring, Mr. Milosevic. Who is it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the lady, 1071, whether she knew that man who told her that her husband had been killed. I asked if she knew his name. But it happens to be irrelevant, because lady 1071 just said, "The man is dead."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I think that much is written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't note that at first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Give me a moment to look for that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in the paragraph 13. The name appears on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But in any case, you were not able to find out from him any more detail, any more information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it all boils down to these three sources, three persons who gave you tidbits of information about your husband. And the only thing that you can precisely know was that he was captured by this group of people outside the cinema.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was a group of civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: So I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Witness, I would appreciate just a couple of clarifications for the benefit of the Judges. About the barracks, this barracks that we're talking about, is it located in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not close to your home, but it is located in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in that town, the barracks existed always, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a big barracks with a lot of troops and a lot of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I don't know. I rarely visited that part of town. And as for the number of troops, I don't know. I think it is a regular, normal building, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that the barracks and the troops inside it at one point remained cut off from electricity, water supply, and food supply.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: They were cut off first, and then the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was cut off to them first and then to the rest of the population. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I only heard about the timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks? Was anybody using weapons to attack the barracks at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did this happen first, before the shelling of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: That's how people told it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Were there any casualties among the soldiers and officers during that blockade, before the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear about it firsthand, because I was in the basement. As I said, I heard about the attacks on the trucks. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam 1071, did the members of the OTP not tell you that there's a witness in this Tribunal that -- who says he had seen the body of your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness C-1071, Mr. Milosevic suggested, as he put it, "It all boils down to three sources who gave you tidbits of information." In your statement, I believe you refer to another source. On page 3 of your statement, you mention how you went to Dalj on the 22nd or 23rd of November, 1991 to begin to look for your husband, and you went to the JNA headquarters in Dalj and you spoke to a guard there. Do you recall what, if anything, that JNA guard said about mistakes that had been made? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I was told at that time, when I asked, whether they had a list or something. This man, this army man, told me that they had made a mistake because they had turned over everything to members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you had heard that the most frequent victims from Vukovar were people in mixed marriages. You were in a mixed marriage yourself, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness C-1071, has your husband's body been found and identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us when your husband's body was found approximately and approximately where it was found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Roughly before the time I gave this statement, in spring 2001, and it was found in a clearing called Lovas, between Dalj and Lovas -- sorry, between Dalj and Borovo Selo, so I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were there any wounds found on your husband's body, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: I was told that he had two entry and exit wounds and possibly other wounds I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what caused the entry and exit wounds, according to what you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1071
utterances.text: Probably gunfire. I don't know. Rounds from a rifle. I didn't ask whether it was a rifle or a pistol. They didn't tell me, and I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1071, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded, and you're free to go. But would you wait until the blinds have been lowered, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, we'll adjourn now. We'll take the adjournment slightly earlier, but it would be convenient, and we'll hear the next witness after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let us deal with the witness first. Ms. Bauer, arrangements have been made for this oath to be taken, have they?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I believe they have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you follow what the interpreters say, please. And if the interpreters would read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we heard a moment ago that this witness Josip Josipovic was taken off the list. I wanted to kindly ask you to find out if Mr. Josipovic had come to The Hague this week. And second, I want to point out that he is providing very important evidence on the events that took place in that part of Bosanska Dubica and Hrvatska Dubica and that I have very good reason to conclude that the side opposite is taking him off the list because his testimony is not convenient to them. Let me just read the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. What we're going to do is this: We're going to hear this witness's evidence first. She's here and she should be able to give her evidence without interruption. We will then return to the witness who you've referred to, and we'll hear about the position then and you can make any submissions. But let us first of all deal with the witness who's in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Do you hear me properly?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Ana Bicanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Ms. Bicanic, do you recall that two days ago you went through your statement in the presence of a representative of the court?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And did you sign a declaration attesting to its accuracy and truthfulness in front of this court representative?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I'd like to offer the statement pursuant to the regulation 92 bis into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get an exhibit number for the package.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'll commence with the summary. Ms. Bicanic was a housewife and 56 years old at the time of the events. All her life, she lived --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Ms. Bicanic, I'm reading out the summary. You don't need to say yes or no. So just sit back and relax, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: All her life she lived in Saborsko, which was a predominantly Croat inhabited village of approximately 7 kilometres in length. From June --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Ms. Bicanic, you don't need to say yes every time I read something out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I should just go ahead, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. From June 1991 to November 1991, Ms. Bicanic observed APCs and jeeps full of soldiers driving through the village towards Licka Jesenica, where the JNA had a military training base. At the foot of a hill called Pljesevica, there was a military heliport, which was located close to Saborsko. Helicopters and planes would fly over the village of Saborsko regularly at that time. In 1991 -- in June 1991, Serbs from the direction of Licka Jesenica started shooting randomly at the village of Saborsko with gunfire and occasional artillery fire. Some ten people died in these initial attacks and several were wounded. Following these initial attacks, a few persons were evacuated from the area, in particular women with small children and elderly, frail people. Heavy artillery shelling of the village began on the 5th of August, 1991 and continued until two days before the fall of the village on the 12th of November. On the 12th of November, airplanes attacked the village of Saborsko, shooting tracers and dropping bombs. The witness and her husband ran into a basement of a family house belonging to Petar Bicanic. There were around 20 people in this basement seeking shelter from the enemy assault, all civilians. At one point, a woman from the village came to the basement which was used as a shelter and told them to flee because the tanks had already entered the town. Only a few young men followed this advice and ran off immediately. Shortly afterwards, the witness and her husband ran into their house, which was nearby, in order to pick up some warmer clothes. Her husband, who had two hand grenades with him and feared it could cost his life if detected, hid them in a haystack. Subsequently, they returned to the basement. After the bombing attack subsided, the group thought about surrendering and heard someone outside the house where they hid say something to the effect "give me some matches." They believed that the Serbs were burning houses and that they were going to be burned alive, so they went outside to surrender. Mrs. Bicanic, who constructed an improvised white flag on a stick, went out first, shouting not to shoot because they were all civilians. She saw two soldiers dressed in Serbian dark grey uniforms and wearing visor caps with a five-pointed red star. These soldiers were heavily armed and spoke with a Serbian dialect. The soldiers threw a hand grenade into the basement of the house and then separated men from the women, searching all the men and taking their valuables and money. Ms. Bicanic saw how her husband was slapped without any reason. He looked terrified and pale. One of the soldiers shouted that they all ought to be slaughtered. Other Serbs stood on the road, searched houses, and took what they could take. Subsequently, they separated the men and took them behind the house. Ms. Bicanic saw how those two soldiers she initially had seen when she had come out of the basement shot and killed all the men with automatic gunfire, including the witness's husband. Subsequently, the soldiers gave the women an ultimatum, that they had to leave Saborsko in half an hour or to be killed as well. The witness returned to Saborsko in 1995 and could not recognise the village. Everything was destroyed and overgrown. The witness's house was completely demolished and burned. Two local churches were destroyed, one completely, the other one from medieval times was heavily damaged. After Operation Storm in 1995, a mass grave was discovered near the parish house in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I apologise. The witness's husband, Milan Bicanic, was among the dead, as well as other men killed with him on that day. I conclude the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bicanic, in your statement, you say that in the year 1990 a referendum was held and that Croats were happy and Serbs were not happy at all about this referendum. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you -- did you hear that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not right. The Serbs were very happy when they were doing this, because that's what they wanted, to have Greater Serbia and to destroy whatever they could destroy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, I understand this explanation after yours, but it has nothing to do with my question. I asked you about your statement, and I will read out from it. "In 1990, there was a referendum and the Croats were very happy but the Serbs were not happy at all."

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Because they wanted Greater Serbia; that's why they were not happy. They attempted to have a Greater Serbia, and that's how it all played out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Bicanic. How do you explain the fact that the Serbs were not happy about the referendum concerning the separation of Croatia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that's why they were not happy.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: They were happy. They got it all. They surrounded places. They killed whoever they wanted. How wouldn't they be happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Bicanic. In the same paragraph you say that "Serbs as early as the summer of 1990 erected barricades on roads."

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of these barricades?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the barricades or the people who erected them, but it was all blocked. We were surrounded, isolated, like we sitting in this room. We couldn't move out. We could use up whatever stocks we had at home, and the few supplies we had in stores until the very attack started. We were surrounded, encircled, like we in this room. We couldn't go out anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But did these people who told you about these barricades ever tell you where exactly they were located?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I didn't go there, and I didn't really interrogate anyone about them. I just heard about these barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But was it in Saborsko itself?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to Saborsko, going towards Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you at least see that one barricade at the entrance to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Did you hear what I said? I didn't move anywhere. I only stuck to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is Saborsko a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Croatian. And there were also four Serbs, four Serb neighbours living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was it the locals, the inhabitants of that village who erected the barricades?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: They had no reason to. They were not afraid of anything. These four Serbs were together with us in that basement and we got on well together until the last moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who erected this barricade in your village?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: These people from Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the people from the neighbouring village?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the neighbours. It's their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. On page 2, in paragraph 3, you say that in the beginning of June 1991, the Serbs started opening fire on your village.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they mainly shot at the school building and the church.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was inevitable. Every house got its share.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Bicanic. What was it special about the school building and the church so that they shot at them?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Well, they were normal, regular buildings. Children went to school. And these two buildings had it the worst, got the most bullets and were eventually razed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were any weapons situated on top of the church and the school building that were targets?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, there was nothing. There were even very few policemen and very few people who had any weapons, and those were small rifles. That was the heaviest weapon anyone had, including the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at that time nine inhabitants of Saborsko got killed.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, from machine-gun fire from a plane. We couldn't stick our heads out whenever we could hear a plane. And if we were out having breakfast, if we happened to be out, we had to move right back in, and these nine people were shot while on the road, from a plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was machine-gun fire from aircraft.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, when planes were flying over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was it exactly, this bombing from planes?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: In 1991. It all happened in the summer, in that period, from August to November. In November we fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say that Saborsko was bombed from airplanes. What was it that airplanes had to bomb in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: How do I know? They wanted to destroy it. It was a small village. There were no troops, nothing. There were only civilians mostly and people defending themselves and standing guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you say yourself, Mrs. Bicanic, on page 3 of your statement, in paragraph -- in the first paragraph, that "Around October 1991, two truckloads of Croatian soldiers with around 50 men arrived."

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. They brought some aid in food and we got some small arms then, and that was nothing; it's a drop in the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 50 soldiers arrived and weapons.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Well, a defence team, a defence force came. Because we were by that time unable to survive. We were afraid we would be slaughtered. We were not expecting so much army to come to our door and attack us. We were unable to defend ourselves because it was such a great force against such a small village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they manage to come with trucks -- on trucks to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: They went through the woods, crept at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they creep on trucks?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Through the woods, because everything was blocked, everything was surrounded. There were guards everywhere. We could see that there was nowhere to run. It was all people from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Bicanic. But did you find out how they managed to reach you by truck through the woods?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: How they managed? They didn't fight or anything like that? Somehow peacefully they managed to get there. They stealthily managed to pass, the way thieves do. They tried to defend it but they didn't defend anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that these two trucks brought 50 soldiers and weapons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, some rifles and some very small weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "small weapons"?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: I mean small arms; rifles and a couple of grenades perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you're quite sure that there were only two trucks, in view of the fact there were 50 men bringing food and weapons, and all this fitted into two trucks?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Two trucks. There weren't more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was there a police station in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many policemen were there there?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Ten or so, and some civilians, a few elderly people. That was all we had to defend ourselves until these men arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these 50 soldiers that arrived, how many members of the TO were there in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Nothing. It's all one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, in the second paragraph, you say that social workers in July 1991 - so this was prior to these events - came to Saborsko and evacuated elderly persons, children, and younger women; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people left Saborsko on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Mostly the elderly, old women and children, and the children's mothers. But these were few. We didn't have that many people in the village. The people who were unfit and who couldn't walk, who couldn't flee, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So those unfit for military service left.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: People who could not run through the woods and small children who couldn't spend the night in the woods. We didn't spend the night in our homes but in the woods because of the shooting and the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me how many inhabitants there were in Saborsko in all.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I don't know. I'm not that literate to know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many people stayed on in Saborsko when these people had left in June 1991, all these women, children, the elderly men, and so on? How many people remained in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: You mean when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How many people remained when these left?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Few. Some soldiers and some people; the elderly women and so on. And they waited for the last moment, until everything happened, until the attack came to destroy everything. And then people started fleeing, who managed to save their lives, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So only the men stayed behind, those capable of military service. All the others had left Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No. Some women stayed behind too and men. Only the -- those who were unfit, who couldn't hide, the children and the old men left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
