utterances.text: Very well. On page 3, in the third paragraph, you say that "Heavy shelling of Saborsko started on the 5th of August, 1991."

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I say "Kolovoz" for August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you say "Kolovoz" for August. And that the only two days when there was no shelling were the days prior to the fall of the village on the 12th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: For three months, from the 5th of August, there was shelling every day and there were helicopters flying over the village to Vukelic Poljana. And as they flew over; we knew that in the evening shelling would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the 5th of August until the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only in -- on the 12th of November there were two days prior to that that were peaceful. And then on the third day, that is, on the 12th of November, after this lull early in the morning, the planes started shelling and they didn't stop until they destroyed everything. That's it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mrs. Bicanic, does that mean that Saborsko was shelled for all of three months?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout a period of three months, they never stopped for a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, you say your husband had two hand grenades on him.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, to save his life. If he were to be captured alive, that he could kill himself, not to hand himself over alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did the others have, in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Rifles. Rifles. There weren't many weapons. They didn't have anywhere to get them from. Maybe from the heavens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when this attack occurred, where were these soldiers and policemen, these 50 soldiers who came?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: They were at positions, deployed. And when the planes came, their weapons and rifles were thrown away and each one of them fled, because they simply couldn't resist such a strong force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, as you explained it. But on page 3, in paragraph 7 you say that the circumstances quieted down that afternoon for two or three hours and that Nikola Bicanic, he was already deceased, that he should surrender.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Nikola was already dead by then. That's not correct. I said that when we were coming out of the woods, when everything was over. We fled from the basements. There was a lull. And at night for three days and three nights we went over there. And Nikola said this in the basement. When there was a lull -- the army had already entered the village, and he said it would be a good idea that we surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: This Nikola in the basement, he said that you should surrender?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that we should come out with a white rag to surrender. Otherwise, we would all be killed down there. And as one was saying, "Give matches to start torching," and one woman had a little boy of five or six and she said, "Take his white shirt as a sign of surrender." This was in my street. I went out and saw two soldiers with those heavy weapons, those big rifles with something around on them. I don't know how you call them. I folded my hands like this and I begged them not to shoot. "There are no soldiers here, only men and women." And he said, "Tell them to come out." So I went to the door and told them, "Come out, come out." And then one by one they came out. One of them threw a grenade into the cellar, thinking that someone was still there. And then in front of the house they put the women under a threshold. Then they slapped my husband first, then Jure Vukovic, also he got a slap. Then Strk, Jure, and then his wife said, "Don't beat him." And he yelled at them. And others were cursing our mothers, saying that everyone should be slaughtered. Outside, there were soldiers, and then these soldiers with five-cornered stars and helmets on their heads -- all this was happening very quickly. They moved about 10 or 15 metres down the road and took a turn at the next corner, and then they opened two bursts of fire, and then they were moving towards us. Again, again I folded my hands and begged them not to hurt us. And then two of them stood in front of them and said, "Where is your son? In the army?" I said, "In Osijek." "Is he in the Ustashas?" I said he was not. "And when did he leave?" I said, "In June." And then they looked at one another and waved their hands, telling us to move on, us women. And I looked in front of me along the main road, and on the main road there were so many soldiers and tanks that an egg couldn't drop between them. Then I called out myself, "Let's go to Jesenica," to Nina. And he said, "Go on." And we ran to this Nina. And as we entered Jesenica, I asked this Nina, "Take us to Jesenica, please." And he said, "Not Jesenica. You mustn't go there. There's no one there. Everyone's been killed." But then there were people coming towards us from Jesenica. I couldn't tell whether they were soldiers or civilians. Mostly civilians. One had a coat over his head, I suppose not to be recognised. And then the others moved off, moved away, and we stopped and a man came towards us and said to Nina, "Nina, where are you going with those women?" And then he cursed, and "I wish I could get rid of them." And then he said, "Women, I don't wish to have your lives on my soul. Just flee. Go through the woods." And that is where we went during the night, until it became more peaceful. And after midnight nothing more could be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, I'm going to stop you now. The accused is going to ask you some questions. If there are any other details which are necessary, then the Prosecution can ask you some questions at the end. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, as far as I was able to understand, many soldiers passed along that road. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the soldiers didn't stop in the village but only passed through. You said there were tanks, trucks. This was an open road and the army was passing through.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and destroying along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they destroyed things as they went along?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they razed everything to the ground. They left nothing behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Those who killed people in my neighbourhood when they found us in the basement, I saw them. I looked them in the eye. They had helmets on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the soldiers passing along the road, what were they doing? All those tanks and trucks and vehicles, did they have anything to do with your village?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Well, they destroyed it, they razed it to the ground. They did what they wanted, and then they went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that one of the soldiers took out a Croatian police uniform from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he said, "Look, this is an Ustasha nest," and he threw it on the ground. This was a police uniform from the police quarters, where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he asked you to tell him who it belonged to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask anything. He just threw it down onto the ground and he said, "Look, here's an Ustasha nest."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: It belonged to a policeman. The policemen used to sleep in that house, but they ran away when the attack started. We fled every which way. Everybody fled as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where did these 50 soldiers flee and these policemen and the citizens?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Oh, they ran every which way, towards Bosnia, towards Slunj, whenever they could. Whoever could find a way out of that hell, fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me who of the soldiers that you knew - because they'd spent a few months there - and the policemen, which of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Quite a few were killed; five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the others fled?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they fled. Whoever managed to do so, to save his life, he fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, how many people were killed in Saborsko in all these attacks?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Are you asking about civilians or altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many people altogether?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: 54 or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this is throughout these three months of bombardment and the attack?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Saborsko is on the main road?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? That they were killed in their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But how many soldiers and policemen were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Quite a few; about 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that a uniform was found there. Did any of your neighbours change into civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No. Why should they? What would they change into?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that some 15 minutes later some men were taken behind the house belonging to Ivan Bicanic. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, my husband and seven men, and they were killed from a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were on one side and they were taken behind the house.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: We were all together, and we were looking at them. There's a road - it's like this room here - and the houses were on opposite sides. And the distance was like from that wall to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 2, you say that you saw those same two soldiers whom you had seen before when you surrendered, that they shot and killed all these men.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: When we surrendered and left the house, they took those men, they slapped them, they took whatever they had in their pockets, then they took them some 10 metres away from us and fired bursts of machine-gun fire at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are the same two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were the only ones whom I saw killing. I didn't see others killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So these two who robbed you, they were the ones who did that?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: How would I know what the others were doing all over the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And after that, you went to a village -- or rather, a Serbian hamlet called Solaja in Borik.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We took refuge there. And Nina went off to Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And there you met other Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you met no one?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no one in that Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No. They were all out in the field, because we took paths through the woods and we hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you wanted to go to Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we were on good terms with them. We weren't expecting anything bad. They were tradesmen. They were teachers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person who prevented you from going to Licka Jesenica, he was a Serbian soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a soldier. He was a civilian and he was together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. There was another man called Bogdan, but we didn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see him on that day but he walked around the village and he was hiding together with us, and he showed us his booklet. He had a booklet which said "SAO Krajina," as he said, and he was there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the man who told you not to go to Jesenica, he said he didn't want to have your lives on his conscience and that you should go and hide.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was a man from Jesenica and he was a civilian. I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. He was wearing civilian clothes. When you speak of the soldiers who carried out this murder --

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- can you describe their uniforms? You said that they had dark grey uniforms on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms and they had white patches, and others had camouflage uniforms without those patches, but the two -- these two, they had the JNA uniforms with the five-pointed star, the ones who committed the murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to say that they had dark grey, as you say, Serbian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No. They were kind of greyish, multicoloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The two soldiers who committed this murder, in your opinion were they members of the JNA or were they reservists or territorials?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: How should I know what they were? But they had military uniforms on. They had real military uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't know any of them?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the other people present on that occasion have any knowledge about these men and who they were? Did anybody else know them?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, no one knew them. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Bicanic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have only two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Ms. Bicanic, at the time of the killing of your husband on that day, when you were hiding in the basement, did your husband have any other weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No, no weapon. These people didn't have any weapons at all at that time, except that they stood guard. They had patrol duty. You know what they did, including my husband? They would patrol at night, because they were afraid. They were afraid that people would be slaughtered, so they found cans --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, let me interrupt you here one moment. I'm talking on the day your husband was killed, did he have any weapon at that time, when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: No. No, no. No, none of them had. Of those seven, none of them had anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Bicanic. That's all I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: ANA BICANIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Bicanic, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give evidence. Your evidence is now over and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can explain the reasons why we have actually not brought Mr. Josipovic today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But we actually can reinstall him, but I will explain the situation first. We have, as you all know, a priority list of witnesses given the time constraints for the Prosecution to present the case. And we had for the first week of -- after the summer break scheduled a huge number of Croatian witnesses, which are of this priority group 1, the absolutely necessary witnesses. Mr. Josipovic was not among them, because his evidence is actually covered already by another witness. But it turned out that several of the priority 1 witnesses, crime-base witnesses from Croatia were not available, and that is why we scheduled Mr. Josipovic. He was actually the only one available. And as he has some -- he has some important evidence, we thought it's worth calling him. Now, after the two trial days this week, we got the impression that there is a delay and we would not get through all the witnesses that we scheduled for this week. And just yesterday we decided to then withdraw Mr. Josipovic from this week, because especially the next Bosnia witness needs to be finished this week and be sent home. But Mr. Josipovic is still here, and he -- the proofing will be concluded this morning and we could call him. But if it is -- if it occurs, he would need to be wrapped around the next Bosnia witness, who actually needs to go back tomorrow, and that's why we actually decided to withdraw him. There's nothing suspicious about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the position is this: That you haven't yet made a final decision about this witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We had made a decision yesterday, but we can reinstall him. It's not a -- it's -- we could call him, but we actually had decided rather not. But now it looks actually that we are much faster than we expected it to be, so the time constraints that we saw for this week seemed to disappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the position is that the next Bosnian witness, who will be the witness after this; is this right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is your last witness today, we understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo is actually the next witness we thought would testify today. The next witness could start, but it would actually have to be Mr. Josipovic, because one of the Bosnian witnesses has fallen sick. She is actually at the doctor's. And the other one is only arriving this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. But did I understand you right? One of the Bosnian witnesses has to finish this week?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely, the male one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let us call this witness, and then we can consider this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we can see how far we get with the next witness. And then if there is enough time, to also have Mr. Josipovic, we are -- we of course would do that, because he is here and available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad that the witness is here, and he will be followed by B-1054, according to the list I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- we'll consider that. We're going to consider it when we've heard this witness, as to the form in which the witnesses will be taken, the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Luka Sutalo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, did you give a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In June of this year, did you review your statement in the presence of an officer of the court and confirm its accuracy except for one minor correction?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the Rule 92 bis package into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it a generic number, please, the next Prosecution exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 520, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now read briefly the summary of the evidence of this witness, including only a very few questions for clarification. Mr. Sutalo is a Croatian inhabitant of Erdut and was 65 years old during the events. In May 1991, he saw that JNA tanks and mortars began to mass on the other side of the Danube River. In July 1991, two weeks before the main attack, the JNA started to fire from machine-guns across the river during the night. A week before the 1st of August, 1991, the JNA shelled the village with mortars. On the 1st of August, 1991, the witness observed JNA tanks entering Erdut. The tanks shelled Erdut as they drove past on their way to Dalj, just south of Erdut. Hearing that many Croat people had been killed in Dalj, the witness and his wife went to Serbia, on the other side Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the Danube River. There he was arrested by the JNA military police, interrogated, mistreated, and beaten, and he was partially held in a factory building over three subsequent days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I have one question in relation to paragraph 11 of your statement, where you mentioned that four or five other men were also arrested at that time in Serbia and among them were Zvonko Tucak and a certain Mata. And my question to you is: What ethnicity did these and the other few men that were arrested together with you have?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: They were Croats. Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue now with the summary. On the 4th of August, 1991, the witness was allowed to return to his house in Erdut but told to attend a meeting in Dvor during which a new government was to be formed. During this meeting, a man who introduced himself as Marko Loncarevic said that this was not Croatia any more, it was now Serbia, and the Croat people could not rule any more and would no longer be part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, in relation to this meeting in Dvor, you said -- it says in paragraph 19 of your statement that a form of local government was to be formed, including members of all three ethnic groups. And my question to you is: What kind of a government was this and did Croatian inhabitants actually participate in any governmental function?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That meeting was convened by Lieutenant Colonel Kosutic. It was attended by Croats, Serbs, and Hungarians. At that meeting, a demand was made by Lieutenant Colonel Kosutic to elect some sort of government that would rule the village, and he admitted himself that it would not be a democratic government but it had to govern democratically. When the people were finally elected, there were Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians; but in the future, Croats and Hungarians were never invited. Only the Serbs were actually on that government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue now with the summary. Over the next several weeks, the witness had to report to the local police on a regular basis and was interrogated frequently. Restrictions of movement were imposed on the witness and others. Houses were searched and looted. On the 15th of August, 1991, the witness was ordered to join a work crew consisting of Croats and Hungarians, repairing the TO facility in Erdut, which was clearly being prepared for occupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I have a question in relation to what you said about the restrictions of movements. These restrictions of movements, did they apply to the entire population, including Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No. The curfew at the beginning was set at 8.00 p.m. And after a month or so, they extended it to 9.00 p.m. The only thing I want to point out is that it only applied to Croats and Hungarians. It did not apply to Serbs. They went wherever they wanted, and we were the only ones who were not allowed to move out of our houses and yards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were houses of Serb inhabitants searched or looted?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No. Only Croat property.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Serbs ordered to work in a work group like you were working in?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Not that I know of. They didn't work. Only Croats and Hungarians worked, chopping wood, picking corn, cleaning stables.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. On the 25th of August, 1991, the witness was arrested while working in the orchard near his house, cutting grass. He was taken to the police station in Dalj and detained in a small room for about a week with seven or eight others. During the night, Mr. Sutalo was interrogated. Although he himself was not beaten, his fellow detainees were beaten. From Dalj, the witness was transferred to a large stable or workshop in Borovo Selo and kept there for several days. When the witness arrived, there were about 80 prisoners there. The detainees were beaten severely on a regular basis and one detainee, a Croatian policeman from Bilje had a "U" cut into his forehead with a knife. The witness and some other detainees were then transferred to the Borovo Selo police station for a few days, where they were kept in a room in knee-deep water. Then they were returned to the previous cell in the Dalj police station. There the mistreatment continued. Most of the detainees were beaten every single night and during the daytime too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I have just one question: In relation to your fellow detainees in Dalj and Borovo Selo, what ethnicity did these other detainees have?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: They were mostly Croats and Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned also a Haso Brajic in paragraph 44 of your statement. What ethnicity did he have?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He was of Islamic faith, a Bosniak who lived in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll continue with the summary. Two or three days after the witness was taken back to the Dalj police station, Arkan came to the police station with several of his men. He introduced himself and cursed the detainees with ethnic slurs. His men beat the detainees while Arkan watched. During the beating, several of the detainees were seriously injured. Towards the end of September 1991, Haso Brajic was detained in -- was taken into the witness cell after he had been severely beaten in the yard. In the night of the 22nd of September, 1991, several men in camouflage uniforms appeared in the cell. One of them asked for the witness. The witness identified himself and the man said, "You are coming with me. I'm taking you home." At that point, Slavko Palinkas, a fellow detainee said, "Mr. President, take me as well." At the time, the witness had no idea why Palinkas referred to the man as "Mr. President." The man also secured Palinkas's release. The witness only subsequently learned that the man was Goran Hadzic. The witness was taken into the yard of the police station, where he saw approximately 30 to 40 men he calls Chetniks, and among them was Arkan. The witness was driven to Erdut. On the way to Erdut, Goran Hadzic asked him if he had been beaten. The witness replied that he personally wasn't but what was happening to the others was horrible because they were beating innocent people. Goran Hadzic asked the witness how he knew that they were innocent and the witness replied that they were men captured in their gardens or fields, just working, and Goran Hadzic said, "These days everyone is beating everyone else." The witness never saw Haso Brajic or any of the other detainees left behind when he was released. After this event, people in the village began to disappear. On Christmas Eve, a bomb was thrown into the witness's yard and caused damage to his house. When the witness reported this event, a commission came to investigate; however, when they found out that the witness was a Croat, they said, "That explains it," and left it at that and nothing happened. The witness applied for a permit to leave Erdut. Before the permit was granted, the witness had to sign over his house and all of his property to the village council.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this -- in relation to this, Mr. Sutalo, I have just two questions: Why did you leave Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, they had begun to mistreat me, to blackmail me, to threaten me, and I realised I couldn't go on living there. I had to run. And even before that some Croats had started to flee because they had been beaten up, threatened, and mistreated, and it was not possible to live there anywhere. You were not allowed to move around. You were not allowed to visit anyone. The only way out was to run. Run where, I didn't know. I was going into total uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And so why did you sign over your property?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, in order to the stay alive, because I had to run away. People had started to go missing, to be beaten, to be detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, was it required to be allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, that was the only way out if you wanted to save your neck. I had to run away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, my question actually was related to the signing over of the property. Did you have to do that to be allowed to leave or not?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, otherwise I couldn't get the document allowing me to leave, to go across the bridge to Serbia. It was a condition, a precondition for obtaining this permit to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I would like you to clarify in what context the photo of the accused is included in this packet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these were just the attachments -- attachments to his -- his statement, and it's actually showing basically photos of Arkan. He was shown -- the investigator showed photos to the witness from which he actually had to say whether he recognised any person, and he did recognise Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was just the recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, just the recognition of the person who he met, as being Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before I start, let us clarify one thing. I apologise to Mr. Kwon, because I haven't quite understood his question. I don't have a photograph in my package. Is Mr. Kwon asking what photograph of mine is included?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Look at the -- the package you should have been given today. You should have just been handed one. Ask you'll see some photographs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I've only just received this before the examination of Mr. Sutalo. I received a package. Yes, at the end there are some photographs. I just can't understand -- oh, I see. This is my photograph. This is a photo montage. It is shot at a funeral. Here in front is my daughter. Right there is a general. This is a photograph from a funeral ceremony at the new cemetery, and I believe it was the funeral of Radovan Stojicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has it got to do with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you heard the evidence. It was shown -- or some photographs were shown to the witness from the point of view of recognition. It was in particular in relation to Arkan. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is it right that the only photograph of significance is the Arkan photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The others we can dispense with?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't understand at all how come that I receive such packages just before the witness comes in. I really have no time to review the documents. I can't see the point of this practice. But let us not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I imagine the documents were probably disclosed to you a very long time ago and also at the time in which the application was made for the 92 bis statement to be admitted. But in this case, there's absolutely no prejudice at all. Yes, let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in view of this remark, I only wish to tell you, Mr. May, that, for instance, for the witness following Josipovic, which is 1054, I haven't got the statement yet. I have checked through my associates; all we received is the transcript. I haven't got even a statement for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course, when we get to that witness. But let's start the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sutalo, is it true that before the elections in 1990, the relations among residents of Erdut belonging to various ethnicities were, as you described them in your statement, "perfect"?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, until the arrival of the Jugo army on the 1st of August, 1991, we lived as one family. In Erdut, there were mixed marriages between Croats and Serbs. We attended each other's funerals, celebrations of saint's day, Christmas Eve, and we lived as one family indeed. When the Jugo army arrived to our village, it was like all the devils had come upon us. They stopped talking to us, they stopped acknowledging us, they stopped all contact with us. Looting began, threats, and all sorts of evil. Even when I was detained by Mr. Kosutic, some colonel - I don't know any more who it was, Milo Savljevic or Rade Savljevic - came to ask me what kind of relations we had between us. And I answered, "Please don't do anything to ruin this. Just let your men stay where they are and everything will be all right." But nobody listened to me. They acted according to the principle "divide and rule."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kosutic, you said, "Since the Jugo army came." I asked you about this because I read your statement, and your statement is your testimony. It's one and the same thing because your viva voce testimony is very little. I'll read out to you what you wrote. You didn't write about the arrival of the Yugoslav army that ruined your interpersonal relations. You wrote the following: "Prior to the elections in 1990" -- I'm reading from your statement. "Prior to the elections in 1990, relations between the different ethnic groups in Erdut were almost perfect. We got along well. We attended each other's weddings, funerals, and feasts. This was due in part to the multitude of mixed marriages we had." And then - I'm not skipping anything - you go on to say: "When the HDZ party was formed, I became its member. Meetings were held in Stjepan Lucan's house in Orasje on the outskirts of Erdut.." And then you mentioned who the president was, and then the next paragraph goes: "After the elections in 1990 --" and I repeat, after at the elections, not after the arrival of any army. You say, "-- the local Serbs stopped talking to us Croats and avoided us. There was no explanation or reason given for this behaviour, but it was obvious that they wanted to cause a rift between us. Although Serbs accounted for only 26 per cent of our population in Erdut, they had the best jobs." So why is it that after the elections -- in fact, first after the establishment of the HDZ party and then all the time you're talking about 1990, why did a rift follow? Why did the relations deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Because when this man of yours, Raskovic, came and held that speech about the Serbs -- or to the Serbs in Dalj - it was a pre-election meeting - he issued -- he distributed those documents to Serbs on how they should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, as far as I know, Professor Raskovic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, which also existed in Croatia in 1990 and ran in the elections.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. But he carried that fuse throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What he carried, I don't know, but he was a Serb from Krajina. He was a renowned psychiatrist or a neurological psychiatrist, I don't know any more. He was the founder of the Serbian Democratic Party in Croatia. And as you well know, we didn't even know him, we in Serbia at that time. And you also know that in your parts, in Eastern Slavonia, most Serbs voted for the League of Communists of Croatia, SHSDP.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know who they voted for. I know how they acted later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know how many deputies they had in the Croatian Assembly precisely from your area, from your list.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could have read about it in the newspapers. There was a list of assemblymen. So when was it that relations deteriorated? When the HDZ came into power or a little before that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, no. After that rally held by Raskovic, it's then that they received instructions on how to act. Because I had a lady neighbour who said, "We are not allowed to talk to you Croats." I asked, "Why?" And she said, "Because we got orders not to talk to you," and that's it. And some Serbs just said in passing, "You Croats are going to come to a bad end, something bad is in the offing for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't you have enough proof that Serbs were not in favour of Raskovic because they didn't vote for his party?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know who voted for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can know that, because his deputies were -- his MPs were not elected there. Let's not waste any more time on this. Let's go on. Do you know anything about what happened from then onwards, from 1990, and how the status of the Serbs changed or how they were treated by official authorities? Let me not specify. Do you know anything at all?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I do. I know that not a single Serb in Erdut was struck, robbed, or threatened before the army arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you say that until the army came. When did the army come?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: When they, Croatian policemen in Borovo, were killed. Then immediately after that, the Jugo army brought its tanks along the road, along the bank of Danube towards Croatia, and they came up to the bridge. And these three tanks stood on the Erdut bridge all the way up to the 1st of August. Around the 10th of July, Jugo army shelled us from Bogojevo and it was our good fortune that nobody was killed. The second shelling was around the 12th of July, and on that occasion seven policemen were killed. On the 1st of August, they moved to invade Croatia. As soon as they arrived, as soon as they crossed the bridge and reached the first populated area in Erdut, they immediately started firing artillery shells. One of them fell into a pigsty of Mate Vukovic and killed a pig. Another one fell into a house, and another one into a neighbour's yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there -- were there any casualties from this artillery fire except that sow?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: There were no casualties. On the first day, they destroyed Nikola Erduat's [phoen] house and another house. I don't know why, because they were offered no resistance. There was no resistance at all. And why were they shooting? They must have wanted to show clearly their intentions to the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not speculate about their intentions now. You said they were responding to the events in Borovo Selo. Do you know that it was precisely the JNA, which you refer to as Jugo army, saved Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo, without firing a single round? Instead, it intervened, diffused the clash, and enabled the Croatian people, who had gone there and opened fire at people, to be pulled out and save their lives. Do you know that, Mr. Sutalo?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly happened. All I know is that 12 Croatian policemen were killed. Why were they killed if there was no resistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you are giving evidence here about Borovo Selo. I was just asking you this question because you mentioned the Jugo army and Borovo Selo. It was precisely in the case of Borovo Selo that this army separated the two conflicting parties and saved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, this is argument which you run with all the witnesses. You see, you complain that he's giving evidence about Borovo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Selo, but you ask it. But in any event, this witness wasn't in Borovo Selo at the time and can give no direct evidence, so there seems little point asking this witness -- or putting to this witness what you say happened or what the role of the JNA was. Now, there may be witnesses who can deal with this more directly, and we'll hear from them. But there's little point putting it to a witness who wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to raise this. The witness himself mentioned the intervention of the Jugo army in Borovo Selo and this intervention is very well known. It was very positive and constructive, because they had stopped the conflict without firing a single round.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, you can say what you please, but the Jugo army is to blame for everything, headed by you. Because if you had said a single word, if you had said "Enough" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, let us confirm the evidence, if we can, and we'll confine the questioning to the matters that you can deal with directly, your own experiences in Dalj and also in Borovo Selo police station. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Sutalo. Where did you get the idea that I commanded the Yugoslav army in 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: You were the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's -- let's not go into that. Now, come on. Let's deal with the evidence which this witness can give directly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm just responding to what the witness says, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Sutalo, that in May 1991 tanks started to build up on the other bank of the Danube, across the bridge, and that local Serbs were seen crossing over.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were suspected of being, as you say here, collaborators. In para 6 of your statement, I read, "Some of them were believed to be collaborators, amongst them Bozidar Purkovic, Jovo Mihajlovic," and so on.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: This Mihajlovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, it was all one and the same country. Our citizens went to the neighbouring Hungary, Austria, Germany, travelled to all European countries. What does it mean "some people were crossing the bridge over to Serbia"? What do you mean "some Serbs went over to Serbia"? Everybody was free to go everywhere, and even you ended up going to Serbia to save your neck.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, but it was with different reasons. This Purkovic, I don't know exactly when he fled, it was 10 or 15 days prior, and he only returned when the Jugo army came. And this other man, Mihajlovic, had spent a lot of time there, and he was trying to recruit other men and he was saying that there would be an invasion of Croatia, and later on he met with some Chetniks. In fact, I didn't see it for myself, but I heard that he had something to do, some connections with the Chetniks, and he was holding some meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was not with the Jugo army, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That is a different thing. The Jugo army was there, and they occupied -- they came to the bridge and occupied us, and all sorts of evil started with that. I don't understand why you keep defending this Jugo army so badly, because you know they are to blame for everything. They had the weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, you're giving evidence. If you would confine your answers, please, to the questions, rather than trying to interrogate the accused. Now, the time has come for us to adjourn. There is one matter before we adjourn, and that's the question of whether you're going to call Mr. Josipovic next. There should be a -- there should be time at least to start his evidence today, and that might be an appropriate course. But let me consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you're prepared to call Mr. Josipovic, we can begin his evidence today. We can interpose the other witness, who has to get away, tomorrow but hopefully finish them both tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We also are in a position to distribute the 92 bis package within this break, I hope. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For Mr. Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because we didn't provide it today because we thought he wouldn't testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Mr. Sutalo, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you please remember, as we warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now, twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: I didn't quite understand you, Mr. Sutalo. What did you have in mind when you say that these men that we mentioned were collaborators?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Because they went over there before the invasion of Croatia, and they returned the day the Jugo army arrived, and they immediately became some sort of commanders in those organisations, which I can call Chetnik or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These two that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of invasion are you talking about? Wasn't the JNA in many garrisons throughout Croatia even before that date?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. But they did what was bad. They beat and opened fire from tanks. Why did they come with 150 tanks to Croatia? Who invited them to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Sutalo. Are you aware of the fact that the JNA never shelled Erdut?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: How can you say anything like that, when it shelled at the beginning of July? Certainly more than 50 shells fell on the village of Erdut, from Bogojevo. And then on the 20th of July, they killed six policemen in Erdut. They fired at least 100 shells on Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that when these policemen were killed?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, but also around the 10th of July some 50 shells were fired on Erdut from Bogojevo, with the VBR. And this was also with the VBR when the policemen were killed. And then every night, from Bogojevo, there were tracer rockets and bullets flying over Erdut. What they were targeting, I don't know, but this was being done by the Jugo army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I see; they were firing over Erdut, not at Erdut.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: How could that be when they destroyed houses and properties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you were explaining a moment ago, no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Not the first time. But the second time, I said that six policemen were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, since you say that on the 1st of August, 1991 at 3.00 you saw -- you heard some shooting from the direction of Dalj. It was indistinct. This continued roughly up until 9.00 or 10.00 a.m., and that the mayor of Osijek came on the radio telling all soldiers to go to defend Dalj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm quoting you. You say, "On the 1st of August, 1991, I heard what sounded like shooting coming from Dalj. It was indistinct. This continued until around 9.00 or 10.00 a.m. The mayor of Osijek came on the radio telling all soldiers to go to defend Dalj," and now you say you don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: There was shooting, but I don't know that the town mayor called on the army to deal with it, but I know that there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what it says here, that the town mayor called for the soldiers to defend Dalj, you didn't put that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know who put it there, but I am not aware that Mr. Kramaric called anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you say that the forces attacking Dalj was followed by another column of some 50 tanks that were shelling Erdut, and then a third group of 50 or so of them entered Erdut. How many tanks did you see in your village?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: There were three columns moving. I counted them. There were 50 tanks in each of those columns. The first, when it passed by, after about seven or eight minutes came the second column. And the second column started firing at the area of Orasje in Erdut. It's a settlement called Orasje. And that is where they started shooting. And then the third group, some tanks went to Erdut and they destroyed Edo Sakic's house and Nikola Jaman's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the JNA was doing there at the time? Do you know that the JNA was endeavouring to prevent a conflict?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: It did not try to prevent the conflict. The third day after they had come, that is, on the 3rd of August, the Jugo army escorted as far as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bogojevo four or five buses of Croats from Dalj. Did they flee voluntarily or were they expelled is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't that an event which shows that they were trying to save the civilian population and to help them remove them from the place of conflict?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Why didn't they protect the Croats, as they did the Serbs? Then nothing would have been needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they did protect them.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, we see how they protected them, when they destroyed houses, looted, and took away everything. We know that best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely the JNA didn't do the looting.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Of course it did. I saw them taking electric engines from the water pump and from various other machines, carrying TV sets. I saw that with my own eyes. At my neighbour's there were four or five soldiers going through the houses during the battle of Vukovar. And then they would carry those TV sets, and they said they would give me one, but they took them away. They took whatever they could get hold of. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that just then the Ministry of Defence took a decision to eliminate paramilitary units and all those that were not part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the period that you are testifying about, there were operations to expel paramilitary forces and to separate the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I do know that in Erdut there was Arkan's office, where there was pre-military training during the former Yugoslavia. He was there. And then he built a wall three and a half metres high, saying that when Osijek fell, he would put Croats there in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone in that camp?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, because Osijek didn't fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was prepared for Osijek.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, there wasn't anyone there because Osijek didn't fall. And anyway, they had expelled all the Croats and Hungarians before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at that time, between June and the 3rd of August, 1992, several tens of thousands of Serbs were expelled?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Where from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From various parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I also know that we were expelled from there and they were put up in our homes, our houses. And I don't know who expelled them, but I do know who expelled us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the municipalities of Novska, Orahovica, Virovitica, 52.000 Serbs -- in fact, up to 60 to 70.000 Serbs were expelled from those areas precisely in that time period.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That is something I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of anything that happened from August 1990, that is, when organised attacks were staged against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many barracks were under blockade in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at least of the siege of the barracks at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: How could I know that, when I'm not from there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were reports to the European Troika and to Lord Carrington, who was chairing the international negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I just know that when Vukovar was captured, they carried wheat from Vukovar. And I know that in one column, going from Croatia to Serbia, 76 tractors left and 32 combine harvesters crossed into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who drove those tractors and harvesters away?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Civilians, Serbs, I suppose. How do I know who was driving them? We didn't dare move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're saying civilians. I see. Very well.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I assume. They weren't Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you're a Croat.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also fled to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I had to flee somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you flee to Serbia when you say Serbia attacked you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, who attacked us? Surely it wasn't the Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you fled to those who had attacked you to save you?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: As soon as we crossed the bridge -- but we couldn't cross the bridge until we received passes. And once we received those passes and showed them at the bridge, then we were able to cross over. And once we were on the other side, we were free. No one asked us who we were or what we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in Serbia, no one asked you who you were or what you were. No one touched you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then on the other side you fought against one another.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: With the blessing of the Jugo army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the Jugo army was separating you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to be quite concrete in connection with what you say, that you were stopped by the military police on leaving the village and that you were arrested and taken to the small factory --

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: The Kudeljara, the rope-making factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You call it a small factory, where your money and documents were seized from you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Personally by Mr. Kosutic, by Lieutenant Colonel Kosutic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't arrest your wife, did they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were not arrested by the JNA but by a local member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No. Kosutic was the most important person then and he interrogated me and he questioned me and he took my documents and later returned them to me. And they tied me up there, to a table. There was a long table, about 10 metres long, and they tied me, Tucak, and this Mata. They tied us to this table. And then they beat them. They didn't beat me, but there was all kinds of things that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You yourself say that two men you recognised, someone called Zvonko Tucak from Erdut and another was Mata from Dalj.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He was a native of Sonta but he worked in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say this was in a rope-making factory. That's paragraph 11. "I was put into a room that had a long table in it," and so on. "I recognised two --" let's not waste time. One was just mentioned. You say he was from Dalj. And both soldiers said, "Sutalo, get up. Come with me. The colonel wants to talk with you." I said, "How can I get up when I'm handcuffed like this," and so on. So these were men whom you knew and who were from Erdut.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Tucak was from Erdut, and Mata was from Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Erdut and Dalj are very close to each other. They're in the same area.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they interrogated you about the Erdut police, about the patrols and so on.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They asked you whether you knew something about the forces, the paramilitaries of the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me questions. I can't remember everything they asked me, but Mr. Kosutic said, "Why did you flee?" And we said, "We weren't running away from the army but we are afraid of Chetniks." And he said, "There are no Chetniks any more. I have disarmed them." And just as he was saying that, a truck full of Chetniks came along, flying a Serbian flag. And I said, "Look at this." And he said, "Oh, dear. Yes, all sorts of things are happening, really."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This only goes to show that this was not under his control.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know under whose control it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you. This is paragraph 12 of your statement: "After a while, Tucak was brought into the room and also questioned. The questioning didn't last long and we weren't beaten." That's what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, we weren't beaten on that occasion, but before that we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say, "A soldier took us to a nearby weekend house, where inside they found my wife and another woman from Erdut named Ivanka Tesanac. I was told we would be spending the night here but we would have to return to the factory for further questioning in the morning."

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were in fact free to go and they were just asking you for information; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Kosutic himself took us to this weekend house. He brought someone from -- it used to belong to someone, a Hungarian called Kabik [phoen]. So he took us to this weekend house and on the following morning we went to see him again. And another Serb came along, a man called Kosta Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sula [phoen]. And he said, "What's Sutalo doing here?" And he said he was locked up, and this man said, "Well, he's an honest man. Why don't you let him go?" And he said, "Well, since Kosta is guaranteeing for you, I'll let you go," and he let me and Tucak and my wife go and they took us home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And in connection with their cursing your Ustasha mother and then later taking you back to Erdut, is it clear that these were people who were not members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: There were soldiers there as well, and they also cursed us. Some of them didn't. Some of them simply asked, "What's going on here?" I asked one of those soldiers, "What were you told when you set out against Croatia?" He said -- there were two of them there, in fact, and one of them said, "They didn't tell us anything." And the other one said, "Of course they did. Didn't they tell us that the Croats were slaughtering Serbs, robbing them, killing them, knifing little children? Our superiors told us all this when we set out for this place."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Sutalo. Is it correct that they searched your house, looking for weapons, and that one of the soldiers found a Skorpion which you say was planted there?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they released you on the 5th of August, and afterwards, as you mentioned earlier, you attended a meeting in Dvor, at which all, as you say, ethnic groups were represented, and the local government was elected, including representatives of all three ethnic groups; Serb, Croats, and Hungarians. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then a man from Dalj said that you were not to remain there any longer, but he was one of the people who was among you. He was one of you. Nobody asked him anything.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: His name was Marko Loncarevic. I don't know what post he held, but he was a member of a Chetnik formation and he was in charge of everything. I saw at that meeting that he was someone who was defending Serbdom. He was one of the founders of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was Colonel Kosutic who was in charge, that he called you together. This is in paragraph 19: "About 100 people were present and all the ethnic groups were represented. A local government was elected. Members of all three ethnic groups formed the government (Serb, Croat, and Hungarian)."

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That's how it was on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Present and in charge of the meeting which lasted about half an hour was Colonel Kosutic who said at the outset that we were there to elect representatives of the government," that it wasn't democratic because there were only about 100 of you there, but those were the circumstances, but that they would have to act in a democratic way. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, but they didn't do that. It was only the Serbs who ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's what happened later. I'm asking you about this meeting which Colonel Kosutic had with you, insisting that you should be part of the local government -- or rather, that it should include both Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the man who said that you were not to be represented in the government had nothing to do with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know. He wasn't wearing a military uniform, and what he was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say -- which is why I'm asking you, because you said something else just a moment ago. I will quote paragraph 21 of your statement: "After the JNA had taken Erdut, there was no curfew or military law." And then you go on to say, "After this meeting, this changed. Telephone and electricity lines were disconnected. There was no radio or television. A checkpoint was set up in every single street, a curfew was imposed," and so on.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: That was on the third day, when they introduced the curfew only for us Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't say that the curfew was imposed only on you Croats, nor could the JNA, if they had patrols in the streets, have been able to introduce a curfew for the Croats only, rather than for all citizens.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Nobody asked me about Croats and Serbs. But now that you are asking me, I'm telling you how it was, because as soon as it got dark and I went outside in the evening, you could hear glass shattering somewhere. You could see cars driving around. And then the looting of Croatian houses would begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was during the curfew. Well, probably that's why the army imposed the curfew, to prevent this happening.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, for us, but they didn't do anything to them, nor did they stop them. On the 24th of December, a hand grenade was thrown in front of my house. I think it was thrown at the house. It was supposed to be thrown into the house, but it hit a metal gate. And I reported this to -- I think his name was Colonel Covic. I reported it to him, and then a military commission arrived, a lieutenant, a captain, and this Colonel Covic, and three policemen from the Krajina also came and three Chetnik -- Chetniks, members of a Chetnik organisation. And they questioned me. They all sat round the table. They all took notes. They took down the information I was giving them and then suddenly the colonel said, "This wasn't meant for you. It was meant for your next-door neighbour." My next-door neighbour was a Serb. And I said, "No, no, Comrade Colonel, this was meant for me." And he said, "I apologise for asking you, but what are you by ethnicity?" And I said, "We are Croats." As soon as I had said this, they all leapt up, took their notes, and said, "Everything is clear now," and they went outside. They didn't punish anyone, they didn't find anyone guilty; I was left without my gate and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure they didn't conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Of course not. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're saying that some people looted houses.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Houses abandoned by Croats who had fled. You yourself gave the example of a man called Gogic who took an excavator, an electric saw. You mentioned a certain Kovacevic, who took a car. All these were local people; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: They were all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were all your neighbours. So this was a local conflict, with looting and so on.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there was looting all over the place. They were all competing as to who would take more. And they took all these goods off to Vojvodina and sold them there, because we tried to find out what had happened to the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were neighbours of yours, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I wanted to establish. So you were questioned there and in the police station in Dalj; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were never beaten.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I myself was never beaten, but the things I saw were terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were not touched and others were beaten? Why?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I'll tell you why: I have a daughter-in-law who's a Serb and she intervened in every possible way. I'm grateful to her, because had it not been for her -- there were 13 of us in Dalj and all were found dead except me and Slavko Palinkas from Aljmas. I would have been one of the dead if she hadn't spoken up for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So out of the 13 of you, 11 were later found dead?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, in Celija, in the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about the prison in Dalj, this prison was not run by the JNA but by the local inhabitants; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: They were not local. I didn't know any of them there, except for Stricevic, who was in charge of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, regardless of whether you knew them or not, it wasn't the JNA who ran the prison.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talk about being taken to the police station in Borovo, where you were insulted. Is it correct that you were visited by people from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not visited by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, we weren't. It was only in Dalj, when we got there from Borovo -- when we arrived in Dalj, we found a girl there who was wearing a blue uniform and on her left side she had a red cross. I don't know who she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As she was wearing a red cross insignia, she was a representative of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you complain to this girl wearing the red cross sign? Did you complain about the conditions?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, we did. When we arrived from Borovo, where we were lying down, then she came with those Chetniks of hers and she carried off the mattresses and the blankets. She carried them off somewhere, so we had to sleep on the concrete floor for a week. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that your son served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, not in the JNA; in the Krajina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He visited you in prison, brought you clean clothes, cigarettes, and so on?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a reservist, a local Croat wearing a JNA uniform.
