utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the JNA. When he came to visit, he was wearing civilian clothes. Whether he was in the Krajina army or the JNA, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You go on to explain what the problems in prison were. Is it correct that the people running the prison had different uniforms than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. They had some sort of police uniforms, and some of them wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, they had nothing to do with the JNA, and yet you go on to explain how you were released and that it was in fact Goran Hadzic who came and released you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did he react when he heard that the others had been mistreated? He asked you whether you'd been beaten; you said no.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've made a note of that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, my son had come to visit me, and he brought me underwear. In a month, we had not been allowed to wash, to bathe, or change. So I sent a message to my son by a Serb to tell him that I was in prison in Dalj, and my son came and brought me clean underwear and a fresh suit of clothes and socks, and then I changed and I lay down and fell asleep. And through my sleep, I heard that something was going on. When I opened my eyes, I saw that everyone was standing. They had been lined up. And so I got up too, and I groped around for my glasses but I was so frightened I couldn't find them. And then I got up and stood in line. And Goran said, "Which of you is Luka Sutalo?" I said, "I am." And he said, "Get ready. You're going with me." I just stood there looking at him. He was to my left, and there were two or three other people there in civilian clothes, and I didn't say anything. He said, "Why are you staring at me? Collect your things. You're coming with me. I'm taking you home." Then Palinkas said, "Mr. President, let me go too. Release me too." And he said, "I am taking Sutalo home. But as for you, I don't have time to take you there." He said, "I have friends in Dalj. I'll spend the night with them." And he said, "All right." And so we went to the police station. The police station was some 4 metres away. It was right next door. When we got there, Goran said, "Get Sutalo's card, get his file." The policeman said, "Sutalo has no file." And he said, "What are you saying?" And the policeman said, "There's no file for Sutalo." And then he swore and he said, "How can you hold a man here without a file?" And he said, "Mr. President, I don't know who it is who's keeping him here. It's not me." He said, "Is there any record?" And the man said, "There's a notebook." And Goran personally crossed out my first and last name in that notebook and he said, "Sutalo, we're going home now." And when we had come outside, I saw 30 or 40 Chetniks outside, and Arkan was with them. They were reporting to him, standing at attention. And he said, "Sit down, Sutalo," and I got into the car and he took me home. During the drive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, I'm afraid our time is limited, and therefore I must interrupt you. If there's anything which the accused wants to ask you about in your evidence, he can do so. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, your time is limited, of course. I think you've got another six minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just finish the story you started, please.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: And as we were going along the road, he asked me, "Mr. Sutalo, did they beat you?" And I said, "No, they didn't beat me, but the rest of the things they're doing, God forbid." "What are they doing," he asks. And I tell him, "You've beaten up those healthy people so badly they're not good for anything any more." And he says, "Everybody beats everybody these days. For instance, when I was at Plitvice, I was beaten black and blue." And I said, "What did you do at Plitvice?" And he says, "Oh, you would like to know too much. I read in a brochure of some English philosopher -- in fact, I said that I read from some English philosopher that it's better to let go 100 guilty men, and he finished my sentence, "Than keep one innocent."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to this scene at the police station when somebody was wondering how come you are keeping these men without a file.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that policeman answered, "I'm not the one who's keeping him. I don't know who's keeping him." So it means it wasn't even the police force. It was a group that had nothing to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I asked this Stricevic, the camp commander, to let me confront this person who is keeping me there. I want to know why I'm being kept here. And he said, "That can't be done and you are not allowed to know that." And I said, "All right, then. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us come back to this incident when a bomb was thrown -- when a grenade was thrown into your yard. Did your neighbours come to visit you and say they were sorry and express their solidarity, Serbs among them?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, some did; some didn't. The neighbour who lived right behind my house, Milorad Gogic, he just alit one morning wearing a military uniform. Another day he was wearing a police uniform. The third day, he was wearing a Chetnik uniform. Let me now ask you, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The one thing he wasn't was JNA.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a uniform, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: People had all sorts of uniforms then. Everybody had one. But that man you saw, that neighbour, he wasn't certainly JNA. Now, tell me something different. You said they forced you to work. There was a question from your examination-in-chief, and you said you cleaned stables. Stables are usually kept by farmers. Does it mean that you went on somebody's farm to work?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, or pick corn every day, without being fed or given a drink all day. You just have to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So whose corn was it?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: It belongs to the Serbs in Erdut. Sometimes you are assigned to go up there to -- there was some sort of administration there who gave us assignments. They said, "You go there and there, and you go to this place," and they just tell you what you are supposed to do and they don't give you anything to eat or to drink. You have to work for free. And then there was this woman -- what's her name? Sucur, Grozda Sucur. She, for instance, went to work -- she went to see somebody in that administration and they asked her, "Why are you going there?" She said, "I want to have somebody pick my corn." And the people asked her, "Who do you mean?" And she said, "Well, these Croats who do all the work. Why not for me too?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you something different. You were free and you were not harmed in Serbia. You were free to move around. But there was one thing that you said before. You signed over your property to the local commune in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: No, Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't keep track of you witnesses, you change so quickly. Dalj, Erdut, it all got mixed up. Now, one thing remains unclear still to me: Was it a precondition for you to sign over your property before they let you go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I believe it was a condition. That man, Bozidar Bolic, who was chief of police in Erdut - he used to be a police officer before that - he said, "We're not going to let you go until you sign a document leaving everything to the local commune." And I got a paper, sealed with the seal of the local community of Erdut. I signed that and then he signed my permit to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it means that this was a man from Erdut, a local policeman, who later became chief of the police at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: He wasn't originally from Erdut, but he worked in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where he was from originally?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, but he lived and worked in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he is the man who said -- wouldn't let you go to Serbia until you sign over your property to the local commune.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sutalo. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This last question asked by Mr. Milosevic was the only thing I wanted the witness to clarify, because I believe this is a very experienced man who knows a lot about a lot of things. You know, Your Honours, that a number of witnesses have already given evidence about having had to sign certain documents before they were allowed to leave a certain territory. Until now, I did not ask questions in this connection, but I believe this witness, Mr. Sutalo, is somebody who can explain this, because he was born in 1925 and he knows very well how these things happen and how property can be assigned from one person to another. And in connection with paragraph 58 of his earlier statement, I would like to ask the following: He said, "I asked for a permit to leave Erdut, which was eventually given me by Bozidar Bolic." And that's the man he just mentioned in response to a question by Mr. Milosevic. I go on to quote: "Before the permit was granted, I had to sign over my house and all my property to the village council."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sutalo, you know very well that according to the laws and regulations of the country in which you lived - at that moment, it was still Yugoslavia at the time - property can be assigned from one person to another or from one legal entity to another only on the basis of court certified documents. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Please, if one Croat per night goes missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Please let me say this. I can't put this any other way. What else would you do if you see the impending doom, if you see the disappearance of the Croatian people, if you see that there is no justice, no one to talk to, no one to ask for justice? And all you can do is save your neck at any cost? I would have signed over my own wife if only so that they should let me go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I understand that much. But let us go back to this document. You know that this document could not have had any legal force. You know that only through a legal procedure and with court certification property can change hands. You do know that.

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes, but my only concern was to escape, to run away from Erdut, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remain alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that much. But do you know of a single person who has signed this document causing a change in the land registry books, changing the ownership? Do you know of any such person?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only two short questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, Mr. Milosevic addressed with you the fact that you fled to Serbia on the 1st of August, when the attack actually started and the JNA moved in. Is -- and you said that you fled over the bridge. Was that the shortest way to get out of the zone of fighting, over the bridge to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: Yes. Because everything everywhere was blocked. I couldn't go to Osijek, because the Serbs had cut off all communication between Krajina and Croatia. In the direction of Vinkovci, Borovo Selo was also cut off. Every communication between one part of Croatia and another part of Croatia was completely cut off. The only exit was via Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in February 1992, when you again left and ran away, as you said, you went to Serbia. Did you stay in Serbia, or did you then continue through Bosnia to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: LUKA SUTALO
utterances.text: I went via Novi Sad to Bosnia, and I crossed over at Raca. I spent the night in Tuzla, and the next day I crossed over into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sutalo, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness, Mr. Josipovic, is here, and we have also distributed the packages in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I don't know if we've got them. We'll call the witness, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Josip Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Josipovic, do you recall that in the years of 2000 and 2002 you gave two statements to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: About two months ago, did you go over these two statements in the presence of a representative of the court and sign a declaration confirming its accuracy and truthfulness?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JOSIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would ask that the statement is moved into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. It's actually two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The package can have a generic number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be Exhibit 521.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: At the time of the events in 1991, Mr. Josipovic was 24 years old. He lived in Hrvatska Dubica in the village of Predore-Cerovljanin. This village, Your Honours, you'll find in the Croatian atlas, page 21, D-3. He worked there as a switchman, a profession he still occupies today. Before the war, Hrvatska Dubica was a town with a mixed population but a slight Croatian majority. Mr. Josipovic described in his first statement the establishment of military formations on both sides in 1991. There was the Croatian National Defence Force, or ZNG, and the Territorial Defence on the Serb side. He explained that the Croats had left the TO after the multi-party elections. The TO headquarters was in Zivaja and the ZNG headquarters in Hrvatska Dubica. Mr. Josipovic participated for one month, in the month of July to August 1991, in the ZNG. He estimated that the total strength of the ZNG force in all the Croat villages, taken together, which would be Cerovljanin, Bacin, and Dubica, were not more than 150 to 200 people. Mr. Josipovic observed as of June 1991 an increased number of JNA helicopters landing in the nearby villages of Zivaja and Sas, which were Serb-controlled villages, delivering ammunition and weapons. Armed clashes occurred during that time involving both sides, however, the ZNG soon realised they could not keep the territory under control and withdrew in early September 1991 As the JNA assisted the local Serb Territorial Defence, the balance shifted in favour of the Territorial Defence. The SAO Krajina police established a police station in Hrvatska Dubica after the Serbs had occupied the territory in about mid-September without too much resistance. Shortly before his capture in mid-September, Mr. Josipovic observed a number of new JNA persons unknown to him who came to the area of Predore-Cerovljanin under the pretext to resettle Serbs who had left the area during the earlier Croat attacks. In reality, local Serbs would sometimes leave to Bosnia for one night but would come back in the early morning hours. In general, Serbs travelled freely between Bosnia and Croatia. Mr. Josipovic had the impression that the JNA assisted the local Territorial Defence and Martic's men in the takeover but then handed the administration over to the local Serbs. He, however, also stressed that the JNA did not participate in the looting and burning of houses. Mr. Josipovic found it difficult to differentiate between Martic's police and the Territorial Defence forces. For Mr. Josipovic, there appeared to be the same. Serbs in the wore were in general olive-green JNA or camouflage uniforms. Those who wore camouflage uniforms had SAO Krajina patches on with a crown and a cross and four Cyrillic S's in the middle. Some of these soldiers were locals; others came from Serbia or Bosnia and Herzegovina. A person called Momcilo Kovacevic was the head of all the Serb forces in the area. Veljo Radunovic was his deputy and was involved with Martic's police. A Serb friend of Mr. Josipovic told him that Radunovic, together with Kovacevic would go to Knin to get instructions from Milan Martic. He also said that it was common knowledge in the area that Milan Martic would be in contact with the local Serb military leadership. Later during his detention, which was in November 1991, Mr. Josipovic learned from two policemen who were imprisoned at the same location that there were some differences developing between Mr. Milan Martic and Kovacevic and Radunovic. Eventually Kovacevic and Radunovic was removed from power. He further heard that the JNA around that time, which means in November 1991, became more proactively involved in the administration of the territory because the army learned of the excesses committed by the local forces. The witness identified during the 92 bis procedure some of the patches he saw worn by Serb soldiers in the area. Some of them have been already tendered as exhibits, and I list the exhibit numbers. That would be 349, tab 12, the Grey Wolves patch; exhibit 349, tab 11, the SAO Krajina patch. There were two new patches, which would have to be assigned new exhibit numbers because in order that they might be part of the patches book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, aren't they tab 22 and 21?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Exactly, we have pre-marked them as tab 21 and 22. They have, however, not yet been tendered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I'd like you to produce the updated list for those patches, the collection of patches and also for the map, Bosnia and Croatia maps. The number is 343 and 326, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes. The number is -- I thought it's 349 of the patch book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, 349 for the patch, and 326, 343 for maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the exhibits can have those numbers which are on the form. Tab -- Exhibit 349, tabs 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: On 15 September 1991, about 50 local Serb soldiers from nearby villages surrounded the village of Predore where the witness had returned. Serbs searched the houses and arrested all male persons, although at that time they wore civilian clothes and did not carry any weapons. The Serbs carried automatic weapons and forced the arrested men to go in front of them in the direction of the river. They used them as human shields to explore Croatian positions. The old man that were initially arrested were allowed to stay in the village. Eight of the others, among them the witness, were brought to the Serb headquarters in Hrvatska Dubica, which was located in the old school building. Five of the detainees, including Mr. Josipovic, were locked in a tiny toilet. There they were beaten by local Serbs, including Momcilo Kovacevic and Stevo Radunovic, three to four times a day. Because of the beatings, the witness lost his consciousness several times. One day, five or six Serbs came and picked up one of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detainees, a Muslim, and led him outside. He heard him screaming and shouting not to kill him. Afterwards, the witness heard immediately shots and this Muslim detainee was never seen again. On one occasion, the detainees were forced to run in circles of -- in front of Serbs for more than two hours singing Chetnik songs and at the same time Serbs beat them repeatedly. They even shot at them without looking if they hit the detainee or not. Because of the beatings, the witness at the end lost again his consciousness when he was hit with a metal bar. While lying on the floor, soldiers would pour water over these prisoners and then marched on top of them. When the witness finally regained his consciousness in the cell, he and another detainee were ordered to carry two dead bodies of two killed persons, Antun Knezevic and Zeljko Abaz on a trailer. However, they were so weak that they couldn't do it and were again beaten for that. Then they were ordered to climb on the trailer and even that was too much. They had to lay on the top of the bodies and saw that the killed people had their throats slit. The trailer was driven over the bridge on the River Una. The detainees were ordered to throw the bodies into the river. But they were too frail to do that. Mr. Josipovic saw how two local Serbs threw the bodies into the river. Around Christmas 1991, the JNA military police, who together with the JNA and not the local Serbs ran at the time the area, transported the witness to Prijedor and transferred him to a detention facility in Banja Luka. He was not mistreated at any of these two locations. In 1992, he was exchanged. The witness lists several names of persons who went missing from his village Cerovljanin and Predore. Most of these people were elderly and did not leave the village, as they did not believe in any threats against their lives. The witness was present at the exhumation of a mass grave in 1997 in Krecane. Many bodies of persons who went missing from Cerovljanin and Predore were identified, but some are missing today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination at the next hearing. Mr. Josipovic, we have to adjourn now, which means that the rest of your evidence will be -- have to be heard tomorrow. We have to hear the evidence for another witness first, but we should be able to get through your evidence, I trust, tomorrow. So if you'd be back then when you're told. Could you please remember this during the adjournment: Not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.51 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 29th day of August, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
